Holds the Main Content screens the study-group conversation pulls into the right-hand panel — the vocabulary self-check, Professor Hale's brief background lecture, the American Yawp textbook excerpt (revealed in three chunks), the note-checking table, the close-reading / grammar tasks, the reading-comprehension check, the lithograph, and the magazine article — plus the vocabulary, Benevolent Empire, and article questions that appear inline in the chat. Launchable so it can be previewed and edited on its own.

READ 1000 — Temperance (FULL SBA): the complete Temperance module, extending the storyboard's authored portion through the parts it left 'in progress'. Across five parts, a study group (peers Danielle, Joe, Karis; reading instructor Professor Booker) works through three texts — an American Yawp textbook excerpt, N. Currier's 1846 lithograph 'The Drunkard's Progress', and a magazine article — building toward a short QUICK WRITE by rating vocabulary, close-reading and highlighting, checking a peer's notes, answering comprehension questions, and analyzing the image, then finally writing four or five sentences comparing the historic temperance movement (the 1800s) with today's approaches to drinking less. Two-pane design: a scripted conversation on the left and a tabbed panel (Main Content / Textbook / Quick Write) on the right. Companion to the storyboard-faithful build (sba/temperance_module_sba).

## Not Just Sober-Curious, but Neo-Temperate

*Shayla Love — published in Atlantic.com, 1/13/2025. As you read, pay attention to the terms* teetotaling, self-optimization, *and* authenticity.

In 1900, a former schoolteacher named Carrie Nation walked into a bar in Kiowa, Kansas, proclaimed, "Men, I have come to save you from a drunkard's fate," and proceeded to hurl bricks and stones at bottles of liquor. The men, interested less in spiritual salvation and more in physical safety, fled to a corner. Nation destroyed three saloons that day, using a billiard ball when she ran out of bricks and rocks, which she called "smashers." She eventually—and famously—switched to a hatchet, using it across years of attacks on what she considered to be the cause of society's moral failings. She referred to this period of her life as one of "hatchetation."

By comparison, U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, an internist of mild disposition perhaps best known for raising alarm about the "loneliness epidemic," has taken a gentler approach to the obstinate challenge of alcohol. His recent call to add cancer warnings to alcoholic products was made without violence or yelling.

The movement of the 19th and early 20th centuries—which eventually brought about Prohibition—went hand in hand with broad religious revivalism and the campaign for women's rights. It considered alcohol to be unhealthy for women, families, and the general state of humanity. The depth of the problem posed by alcohol in pre-Prohibition America is hard to fathom: In 1830, Americans drank three times the amount of spirits that we do today, the equivalent of 90 bottles of 80-proof booze a year. As distilled liquor became widely available, men were wasting most of their wages on alcohol and staying out all night at saloons, and what we now call domestic abuse was rampant, the food historian Sarah Wassberg Johnson told me. Members of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union saw themselves as a progressive group helping the disadvantaged. "They were protecting the home, protecting the family, and protecting the nation by getting rid of alcohol," Dan Malleck, a health and sciences professor at Brock University, told me. In the latter half of the 19th century, young people signaled their moral virtue by taking temperance pledges.

Today's sober-curious, by contrast, post on Instagram about how Dry January has reduced their inflammation, sharpened their jawline, and improved their sleep score. The sanctity of the home, or the overall moral health of society—not to mention the 37 Americans who die in drunk-driving crashes every day—appears to be less of a concern. (To be fair, this focus on health is partially a response to research on moderate alcohol consumption's detrimental effects on heart health, cancer risk, and lifespan.) In a 2020 Gallup poll, 86 percent of respondents said that drinking alcohol was morally acceptable, an increase from 78 percent in 2018. By contrast, more than half of young adults surveyed in 2023 expressed concerns about the health risks of moderate drinking.

Colleen Myles, a professor at Texas State University who studies how alcoholic drinks change cultures, told me that such responses don't mean that the national conversation about alcohol has abandoned morality—simply that Americans' ethical center of gravity has drifted. She considers modern teetotaling to be steered by a great moral project of our age: self-optimization. In her book *Sober Curious*, Ruby Warrington wrote that lower alcohol intake "is the next logical step in the wellness revolution." Myles said that choosing not to drink in an alcohol-soaked culture is seen as an act of authenticity or self-care; social change, but enacted through the individual. In 2019, a nonalcoholic-spirit producer, who calls her product a "euphoric" instead of a mocktail, almost echoed Carrie Nation when she told The New York Times, "Alcohol is a women's lib issue, an LGBTTQQIAAP issue, a race issue." But her vision of temperance was much less socially minded: Sober-curiosity, she said, was about a person's "freedom to choose." One can hardly imagine Congress or a radical activist like Nation attempting to restrict that freedom by outlawing the sale of espresso martinis. The proposed warning label, however, with its nod to individual health (and absence of radical social action), is more fitting for our age of wellness. It won't cure society of all its ills, but it at least has a shot of persuading some people to tone down their drinking.

profile.bio: Thoughtful and willing to weigh in and challenge ideas. Keeps the group on task and makes good judgments about what matters, though she does not always have the full picture.
Curious and honest about what he does not know. Offers reasoning and background, but his notes and reasoning are sometimes flawed — and he is open to being corrected.

Brought up temperance for today's class. Because her sister has struggled with alcohol, she has read about alcohol abuse and its history and often has useful background knowledge — though she is careful to say she is not an expert.

The simulated reading instructor. She sets the group's tasks — the vocabulary self-check, the readings, and the vocabulary and comprehension exercises — and then lets the group work through them together.
The simulated history instructor who wrote the background lecture on the temperance movement. Her lecture is one of the module's texts.
A member of the study group who often speaks for the group.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Hey, Karis. Hey, Danielle.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Hey. Before class starts, can I run something by you? It's about temperance — our topic today.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Sure. But, uh… what even is temperance? I feel like I should already know.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: What do YOU think it has to do with?

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I looked it up — it means holding yourself back from something. The history part is that the temperance movement tried to get people to stop drinking alcohol, or at least drink less.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Huh. Interesting topic for a reading class.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I actually know a little about it — my family's dealt with some of the alcohol stuff. So ask me if it helps. I'm no expert, but maybe I can ask the right questions.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Good to know. OK — here's Professor Booker.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Before we read, take a look at some words you'll meet in the texts. I'm not grading this — I just want to know how familiar each one is. Fill out the table on the right.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: I knew about half of those. Should I look the rest up before we read?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: We'll get to vocabulary exercises later. First, a little background — Professor Hale sent a short note to set up the reading.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Let's read Professor Hale's background on the right — quick context before we get to the textbook.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I knew some of the religious part — the Second Great Awakening. I didn't know about the industrialization angle, though.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Now the reading that matters most for our quick write: the textbook chapter. Here's the first part — read it on the right and highlight as you go.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: I'm confused — what did it mean for "traditional" Protestant Christianity to be "at low tide," and why did that matter?

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Think back to Professor Hale's lecture — she talked about the changes the Industrial Revolution brought, and how some were hard for people to adjust to. For a lot of people, faith was a way to deal with hard things.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: And from the lecture, the main point about Protestantism is that it was the largest religious group in the U.S. — but it also held different values than other groups, like Catholics.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Let's build some vocabulary from this part. Look at the highlighted sentence on the right for each word.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: First one — what does "commerce" mean here?

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Next: antidote. I looked it up, and here are the definitions I found.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: I think you pasted in a couple of definitions for "anecdote," not "antidote."

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Oops. Sorry about that.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Plus, that's a tricky one — one of the meanings of "antidote" IS "a medicine that saves you from poison," but that's not how it's used in the textbook chapter.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Yeah, I see that. In the textbook, they don't mean an actual medicine — it's something that counteracts a harmful situation.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: One more from this part — "proliferated."

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Here's the next part of the chapter.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Now I'm kind of stuck. The people here are middle-class evangelicals — especially women. I get the classes — upper, middle, working — but I've heard "evangelical" without really understanding it.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: From the lecture, evangelicals are a group within Protestantism who emphasized the Bible and sharing their faith — not one specific church or organization. The groups from the last paragraph, like the American Bible Society, were evangelical.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: I'm interested in what the textbook says about women. I can imagine how, back then, men drinking heavily caused problems that really affected women's lives.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Now a term that's special to history. Look at the chapter title — can you guess it?

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Benevolent Empire!

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: The chapter's title points to it. Using the passage, which phrase most directly tells us what it was?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: The phrase that captures it is "a powerful network." What else in the chapter connects to it? Select all that apply.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Now put it together. Each of you wrote a one-sentence definition — read them and pick the best.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: On to the next part of the excerpt.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Wow — whiskey cheaper than milk and safer to drink than water? I just filled my bottle at the drinking fountain before class for free.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I'm remembering that Professor Hale said that before the temperance movement, people drank about three times as much alcohol as they do today. This kind of helps explain why.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: There's a word here — "galvanized." I looked it up, and there are a bunch of definitions. Which one is right in this context?

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I picked "to stimulate or excite as if by an electric shock."

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Me too. That's the figurative definition — they didn't really shock anyone or coat them in metal!

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: I also jotted some notes on the chapter so far. Can you check them? And even if something's right, is it important enough to use in our quick write?

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Here's my list. Sort each statement on the right, then press Check.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: One of those is off, Joe. The textbook said the Industrial Revolution LED TO the social problems. It wasn't a response to them.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Ah — good catch. Thanks.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Lyman Beecher's role in the movement and when those reform societies were growing are good pieces of information, but they're details. The network, the Awakening, and the women's role are the ideas that belong in our final summary.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Here's the last part of the excerpt. These next few words are a kind of paraphrasing — find words that could take the term's place without changing the meaning.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: I'll start — what could replace "eradicating"?

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: How about "exacerbated"?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: One more — "per capita."

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Can we look again at the sentence I highlighted — "Such intrusions by the Protestant middle class exacerbated class, ethnic, and religious tensions"?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: A good sentence to analyze. On the right, each part of the sentence is marked — decide which is the subject, which is the verb, and which is the object.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Notice the subject is a noun phrase. Highlight its parts next — the premodifier, the head noun, and the postmodifier.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Here's the whole structure laid out on the right.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Wait — what intrusions is it even talking about?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Good question. We need the antecedent. On the right, highlight the earlier sentence that describes the intrusions.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: So, using that, why did those intrusions "exacerbate" tensions?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Let's check your understanding of the excerpt with a few questions.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Nice work on the chapter. Before we bring in a modern article, let's look at an image from the temperance era itself — it connects directly to what we just read. Take a look on the right.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Whoa — it's like a staircase of a man's whole life, going up and then crashing down.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Look closely at the nine steps, then answer.

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: Grim. Why would the temperance folks make something like this?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Images like this were made to persuade. Now here's a recent magazine article that connects the temperance era to today. Read it on the right and highlight as you go.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: Wow — Carrie Nation really went after those saloons.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Ha — she'd have fit right into the temperance movement. Dr. Booker wanted us to think about "self-optimization." But first, this word:

body.speaker: Joe
body.text: So, teetotaling — not drinking at all. Where does "self-optimization" come in? Let's each find a sentence that gives it context, then pick the best.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: The line that really pins down self-optimization is the one about not drinking being an act of authenticity or self-care. Put it with the bit about posting on Instagram about inflammation, jawlines, and sleep scores, and you can see it's about focusing on your own health.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Now, to see how it all fits, let's summarize. Which is the best summary of the article's first paragraph?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: One more term the article flags — "authenticity."

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Now step back from the details. What is the article's main point overall?

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: So underneath, the old movement and today's movement are actually pretty different.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: Let's pull all three texts together. On the right, sort each description under the movement it fits, then press Check.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Each of us also tried to sum up the big difference in one sentence. Whose comparison is best?

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: You're ready for the goal we set at the start — your quick write. On the right, write four or five sentences comparing the historic temperance movement with today's approaches to drinking less. Draw on the textbook, the article, and the lithograph.

body.speaker: Professor Booker
body.text: That's the comparison we've been building toward all along.

body.speaker: Karis
body.text: We actually turned all this into a real quick write. Thanks for working through it with me, everyone.

body.speaker: Danielle
body.text: Anytime. See you in class.

## Professor Hale's Lecture

*Background on the temperance movement. Read carefully and use the highlighting tools to take notes — focus on the main concepts and the key vocabulary.*

You may be familiar with Dry January or movements today to encourage people to drink less. This is not a new idea, though what you observe today is in some ways very different than what we will encounter in the texts we will look at. I want you to think about why.

We are talking about the temperance movement beginning before the mid 19th and spanning to the early 20th century. This was a massive set of campaigns aimed at getting people to drink less or to not drink at all.

It is important to understand a few of things about this period. One was industrialization—the growth of railroads and major industries in the US. Another was general sense among people in America that as the country developed, society could be improved. There was also religious revival—you will see a reference in your reading to the Second Great Awakening. This was a wave of increased interest in devotion to Christian faith, particularly among Protestants. This term generally refers to groups that split from the Catholic Church in Europe in the 1500s. If you drive around most cities or towns in America today, you will see several churches—a few will be Orthodox or Catholic, but most will be Protestant. You will also see the term evangelicals. This usually refers to Protestants who place strong emphasis on the importance and accuracy of the Bible and on bringing other people to join their faith. So, as interest in Protestant Christianity grew, more people felt that religious moral convictions could be used to address society's problems.

A major problem was alcohol consumption—in the early 1800s, Americans consumed three times as much alcohol, per capita, as they do today. And there were consequences. Many men spent their earnings at saloons, taking needed resources from their families. And while far fewer women worked outside of the home, there were growing women's rights movements. Many of the same women working for women's suffrage, the right to vote, also supported temperance. In fact, one notably strong organization was the WCTU (Women's Christian Temperance Union). While other movements for the improvement of society made important differences, none were as large or had as great of impact as the temperance movement.

**"The Drunkard's Progress, from the first glass to the grave"** — N. Currier, 1846.

The nine steps, in order:

1. A glass with a friend.
2. A glass to keep the cold out.
3. A glass too much.
4. Drunk and riotous.
5. The summit attained. Jolly companions. A confirmed drunkard.
6. Poverty and disease.
7. Forsaken by friends.
8. Desperation and crime.
9. Death by suicide.

*Beneath the arch, a woman and child leave a ruined home.*

## American Yawp, Chapter 10 (continued)

### The Benevolent Empire

*Read carefully and use the highlighting tools to take notes.*

Because of the Industrial Revolution, middle-class evangelicals had time and resources to devote to reform campaigns, where they exercised their sense of moral superiority over the working-class rabble and the privileged upper-class to try and create a respectable, hard-working middle-class culture. Middle-class women, in particular, played a leading role in reform activity…These women came together in order to deal with issues that primarily affected women and children, such as alcohol abuse, education reform, prostitution, gambling laws, and health reform.

## American Yawp, Chapter 10

### The Benevolent Empire

*Read carefully and use the highlighting tools to take notes.*

In the years immediately following American independence, "traditional" Protestant Christianity was at low tide, while the Industrial Revolution had led to a host of social problems associated with urban growth and large-scale commerce. The Second Great Awakening was in part a spiritual response to such changes, revitalizing Christian spirits while also providing an institutional antidote to the insecurities of a rapidly changing world by inspiring both personal and social reform. These new societies proliferated in the United States between 1815 and 1861, melding religion and reform into a powerful network known as the Benevolent Empire, which included such organizations as the American Bible Society, the American Home Missionary Society (which organized domestic missions within the U.S.), the American Temperance Society, and the American Tract Society.

## American Yawp, Chapter 10

### The Benevolent Empire

*Read carefully and use the highlighting tools to take notes.*

Among all the social reform movements associated with the benevolent empire, the temperance crusade was the most successful. Championed by prominent preachers like Lyman Beecher, the movement's effort to curb the consumption of alcohol galvanized widespread support among the middle class. Alcohol consumption became a significant social issue after the American Revolution. Commercial distilleries produced readily available, cheap whiskey that was frequently more affordable than milk or beer and safer than water, and hard liquor became a staple beverage in many lower- and middle-class households. Consumption among adults skyrocketed in the early nineteenth century, and alcoholism had become an endemic problem across the United States by the 1820s. As alcoholism became an increasingly visible issue in towns and cities, most reformers escalated their efforts from advocating moderation in liquor consumption to full abstinence from all alcohol… They also influenced lawmakers in several states to prohibit the sale of liquor.

## American Yawp, Chapter 10

### The Benevolent Empire

*Read carefully and use the highlighting tools to take notes.*

In response to the perception that heavy drinking was associated with men who abused, abandoned, or neglected their family obligations, women formed a significant presence in societies dedicated to eradicating liquor. Temperance became a hallmark of middle-class respectability among both men and women and developed into a crusade with a visible class character. Temperance, like many other reform efforts, was championed by the middle class and threatened to intrude on the private lives of lower-class workers, many of whom were Irish Catholics. Such intrusions by the Protestant middle class exacerbated class, ethnic, and religious tensions. Still, while the temperance movement made less substantial inroads into lower-class workers' drinking culture, the movement was still a great success for reformers. In the 1840s, Americans drank half of what they had in the 1820s, and per capita consumption continued to decline over the next two decades.
